content: In developing countries, diarrhoea is a significant cause of child mortality, leading to approximately 500,000 deaths annually. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) recommend zinc supplementation as a treatment during episodes of acute diarrhoea. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of oral zinc supplementation in children with acute or persistent diarrhoea. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and contacted experts to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing oral zinc supplementation with placebo in children aged one month to five years. The primary outcomes assessed were the duration and severity of diarrhoea. Data were analyzed using statistical methods, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 33 trials involving 10,841 children met the inclusion criteria. Most of these trials were conducted in Asian countries with a high prevalence of zinc deficiency. Acute Diarrhoea: There is insufficient evidence to determine whether zinc supplementation during acute diarrhoea reduces mortality or hospitalization rates (very low certainty evidence). In children older than six months, zinc supplementation may reduce the average duration of diarrhoea by approximately half a day (mean difference [MD] −11.46 hours, 95% confidence interval [CI] −19.72 to −3.19; low certainty evidence). It probably reduces the number of children whose diarrhoea persists beyond seven days (risk ratio [RR] 0.73, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.88; moderate certainty evidence). In malnourished children, the effect of zinc supplementation appears more pronounced, reducing the duration of diarrhoea by about one day (MD −26.39 hours, 95% CI −36.54 to −16.23; high certainty evidence). In children younger than six months, zinc supplementation likely has no significant effect on the mean duration of diarrhoea (MD 5.23 hours, 95% CI −4.00 to 14.45; low certainty evidence) or the number of children with diarrhoea persisting beyond seven days (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.54; low certainty evidence). None of the trials reported serious adverse events. However, zinc supplementation was associated with an increased risk of vomiting in both age groups: Children older than six months: RR 1.57, 95% CI 1.32 to 1.86 (moderate certainty evidence). Children younger than six months: RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.05 to 2.24 (moderate certainty evidence). Persistent Diarrhoea: In children with persistent diarrhoea, zinc supplementation probably reduces the average duration of diarrhoea by approximately 16 hours (MD −15.84 hours, 95% CI −25.43 to −6.24; moderate certainty evidence). Conclusions: In regions with a high prevalence of zinc deficiency or malnutrition, zinc supplementation may benefit children aged six months or older. Current evidence does not support the use of zinc supplementation in children younger than six months, in well-nourished children, or in settings where the risk of zinc deficiency is low.
